name: South Ridge / Standard Scramble

pitch_detail.notes: Established trail through old-growth forest with switchbacks. ~5 miles roundtrip to maintained trail terminus (5,400 feet). Forest section may be muddy in late spring.
Off-trail scrambling through heather, talus, and alpine meadow. Route-finding required. Climbing directly toward snowfield below West Peak. Loose talus requires careful footing.
Steep permanent snowfield traverse (~400-500 vertical feet) requiring ice axe and crampons/microspikes. This is the crux pitch; fall here is potentially fatal. Angle ~40-45 degrees.
Summit scramble on exposed Class 2 terrain. Final 100-150 vertical feet to the East Peak summit. No technical rock climbing but scrambling is exposed with 500+ foot drops nearby.

descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route - reverse the ascent line exactly. Downclimb the mixed snow/rock crux back to the col, climb back over (or bypass around, staying off the cornices) the West Peak false summit, and regain the boot path down to the official trail terminus near 5,600 ft. From there, follow Goat Mountain Trail #673's switchbacks back down through the meadows, past the wilderness-boundary/Old Goat Trail junction, and through the old-growth section to the trailhead. Carry an ice axe and know self-arrest for both directions of travel on the snow sections: afternoon sun can soften the snowfields significantly (increasing slip and post-holing risk on the way down), while morning refreeze can leave the same slopes firm enough to want careful cramponing. Give cornices along the ridge crest a wide margin on the way down as well - they are easy to underestimate from above and have caused parties to detour off-route.
approach: From the Goat Mountain Trailhead (day-use parking just off FS-32/Hannegan Pass Rd, ~2.1-2.3 mi up from the Glacier Public Service Center), follow Goat Mountain Trail #673. It's a well-built but relentlessly steep trail that gains the ridge via dozens of switchbacks, crossing a small cascading creek/waterfall repeatedly in the first mile through old-growth fir and hemlock (look for ~100-year-old fire-scarred cedar snags). Around 1 mi (~3,200 ft) the grade eases and the trail traverses onto a narrow side-hill ridge. At roughly 2 mi the trail crosses into Mount Baker Wilderness; just past the boundary sign an unsigned spur ('Old Goat Trail') splits east toward an old lookout site - stay on the main tread. Big views of Baker, Shuksan, and Sefrit open through meadows by 2.7 mi, and the maintained trail tops out on the ridge crest at a 5,200-ft viewpoint knob around mile 4, with the official terminus near 5,600 ft (~4.1 mi, ~3,100 ft gain). Beyond this point the route leaves maintained tread and becomes an open ridge boot path: continue about 0.8 mi and 1,000 ft more to the ~6,600-ft West Peak false summit. Snow lingers here well into summer (reports note solid snow from ~4,300-4,500 ft), so carry an ice axe from around that elevation upward, and expect crampons or snowshoes to be useful in early/late season. Do not push straight over the false summit's top - it corniced and exposed; bypass it on the south or west slope. Past the false summit the ridge drops roughly 300 ft into a notch/col, then climbs the final stretch of mixed snow, rock, and short exposed steps to the true (East) summit at 6,892 ft. A narrow, moderately exposed knife-edge-ish section near the top is the crux of the scramble - keep the axe in hand and self-arrest-ready on the steep snow. There is no reliable water source beyond the creek crossings in the forest (roughly the first 2.5 miles of trail); carry what you need for the ridge and summit push.
overview: A twin-summited peak in the Skagit Range of the North Cascades, directly across the Nooksack River valley from Mount Shuksan and just south of Mount Larrabee, within the Mount Baker Wilderness. The standard route follows USFS Trail #673 through old-growth forest and heather meadows to a ridge crest, then continues off-trail up a steep, loose scramblers' path to the false (west, ~6,600 ft) and true (east, 6,891 ft) summits. It's popular both as a strenuous day hike/scramble and as a backpacking or spring ski-touring objective, and is one of the first Baker Highway trails to melt out each year because of its south exposure.
beta: This route continues past the West Peak false summit to the higher East Peak (6,891 ft), the mountain's true summit. The maintained trail ends on the shoulder near 5,400-5,600 ft; everything above is unmaintained boot path and open scrambling. The route involves a steep permanent snowfield traverse requiring an ice axe at all times, then a short, relatively straightforward scramble to the top. The route offers commanding views of Mount Baker, Mount Shuksan, Mount Sefrit, and the surrounding North Cascades peaks.
gear: bear-resistant food storage (canister or hang) in the Mount Baker Wilderness
